Here follows a promise of restoration. Even the sore chastisements coming on Judah would fail to reform its people; God's returning goodness alone would effect this, to show how entirely of grace was to be their restoration. The restoration of her erring sisters is mentioned before hers, even as their punishment preceded her punishment; so all self-boasting is excluded [Fairbairn]. "Ye shall, indeed, at some time or other return, but Moab and Ammon shall return with you, and some of the ten tribes" [Grotius].<div eID="gen20322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20323" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bring again ... captivity--</hi>that is, change the affliction into prosperity (so <reference osisRef="Job.42.10">Job 42:10</reference>). Sodom itself was not so restored (<reference osisRef="Jer.20.16">Jr 20:16</reference>), but Ammon and Moab (her representatives, as sprung from Lot who dwelt in Sodom) were (<reference osisRef="Jer.48.47">Jr 48:47</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.49.6">49:6</reference>); probably most of the ten tribes and the adjoining nations, Ammon and Moab, &c., were in part restored under Cyrus; but the full realization of the restoration is yet future; the heathen nations to be brought to Christ being typified by "Sodom," whose sins they now reproduce (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.32">De 32:32</reference>).<div eID="gen20323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20324" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">captivity of thy captives--</hi>literally, "of thy captivities." The sense here thus is, Thou shalt be restored when Sodom and Samaria are, but not till then (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.55">Eze 16:55</reference>), that is, never. The promise here bursts forth unexpectedly like the sun from the dark clouds. With all her forgetfulness of God, God still remembers her; showing that her redemption is altogether of grace. Contrast "I will remember," with "thou hast not remembered" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.22">Eze 16:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.43">43</reference>); also "My covenant," with "Thy covenant" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.61">Eze 16:61</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.106.45">Psa 106:45</reference>); then the effect produced on her is (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.63">Eze 16:63</reference>) "that thou mayest remember." God's promise was one of promise and of grace. The law, in its letter, was Israel's (thy) covenant, and in this restricted view was long subsequent (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.17">Ga 3:17</reference>). Israel interpreted it as a covenant of works, which she while boasting of, failed to fulfil, and so fell under its condemnation (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.3">2Co 3:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.6">6</reference>). The law, in its spirit, contains the germ of the Gospel; the New Testament is the full development of the Old, the husk of the outer form being laid aside when the inner spirit was fulfilled in Messiah. God's covenant with Israel, in the person of Abraham, was the reason why, notwithstanding all her guilt, mercy was, and is, in store for her. Therefore the heathen or Gentile nations must come to her for blessings, not she to them.<div eID="gen20333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20334" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">everlasting covenant--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.37.26">Eze 37:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.5">2Sa 23:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.55.3">Is 55:3</reference>).
